title: The case for 'working-class liberalism'
gist: Nobel laureate economist Daron Acemoglu argues liberal democracy's post-1980 legitimacy crisis stems from the collapse of shared prosperity for non-college workers plus centre-left parties' pivot to cultural politics, and proposes a new 'working-class liberalism' built on local governance plus redirecting AI toward augmenting worker productivity rather than pursuing AGI.

themes.theme: Diagnosis: why liberal democracy is losing legitimacy

insights.claim: The industrialised world's governability crisis is driven by two linked phenomena: the collapse of shared prosperity for non-college-educated workers since 1980 (most severe in the US, but increasingly visible in Europe too), and a shift by centre-left parties toward cultural politics as their base became more university-educated.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Frames a durable macro/political thesis: as long as non-graduate labour markets remain hollowed out, populist-nationalist parties will keep gaining ground regardless of GDP growth headlines -- relevant to political-risk models pricing populist policy shocks (trade, immigration, tax).

insights.claim: As university-educated professionals gained economic and social status in the computerised, globalised economy, they became more influential within centre-left parties (UK Labour, European social democrats, US Democrats) that historically drew core support from lower-educated manual workers, causing those parties to de-prioritise bread-and-butter jobs/inequality issues in favour of identity and oppressor-oppressed framing.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism behind centre-left electoral erosion among working-class voters across multiple democracies -- useful for forecasting which parties are vulnerable to populist-right gains in upcoming elections.

insights.claim: Neither a return to conservative politics nor authoritarian right-wing populism solves the underlying problem: anti-establishment/authoritarian parties in power are 'plunging into arbitrary policymaking and widespread corruption' rather than addressing inequality or job shortages.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: A direct claim that populist governments (a growing share of the G20/G7 electorate) will underperform on delivery even as they win elections, implying continued governance volatility and policy unpredictability risk premia in markets governed by such administrations.
insights.quote: Anti-establishment and authoritarian parties are not just failing to rise to the challenges that brought them to power, but are plunging into arbitrary policymaking and widespread corruption.

insights.claim: 20th-century social democracy depended on preconditions -- strong unions, an industrial economy, limited capital mobility, and culturally/economically less divided populations -- that no longer hold today, meaning the old social-democratic governing model cannot simply be revived.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Implies that policy nostalgia for mid-20th-century labour/welfare-state models (e.g. reviving strong industrial unions) is structurally mismatched to today's globalised, high-capital-mobility economy and likely to underdeliver.

themes.theme: Working-class liberalism: the two-pillar governing philosophy

insights.claim: Acemoglu proposes 'working-class liberalism' as a new governing philosophy built on two pillars: (1) greater emphasis on local governance to accommodate cultural heterogeneity (on religion, community priorities) while still protecting individual liberties and the 'right of exit,' and (2) prioritising jobs and shared prosperity.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: A named, citable framework ('working-class liberalism') that policymakers and think tanks are likely to reference going forward -- worth tracking as a potential platform plank for centre-left repositioning in the US and UK.

insights.claim: Acemoglu argues unions alone cannot deliver shared prosperity if technology moves quickly toward mass automation, because higher wages achieved through union bargaining would simply accelerate the incentive to automate further.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: A specific, counterintuitive claim: labour-friendly wage policy can backfire by hastening automation -- relevant for evaluating minimum-wage/union-strengthening proposals' second-order effects on automation capex and labour-substituting AI adoption.

insights.claim: Shared prosperity depends on redirecting AI to expand worker capabilities and workplace productivity rather than chasing 'the amorphous dream of artificial general intelligence' -- Acemoglu explicitly frames AGI pursuit as a distraction from pro-worker AI development.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: A prominent economist publicly positions AGI-focused R&D spend (the dominant strategy of major AI labs) as misaligned with broad-based economic benefit -- a contrarian framing investors in AI-labor-augmentation startups vs. frontier-model labs should note.
insights.quote: Shared prosperity depends on redirecting AI so that it becomes a tool for expanding worker capabilities and improving productivity in workplaces, rather than chasing the amorphous dream of artificial general intelligence.

insights.claim: Acemoglu recommends specific policy levers to redirect AI toward pro-worker outcomes: removing the asymmetric tax treatment of capital, increasing competition in the tech sector, and government-sponsored high-profile competitions for pro-worker AI technologies paired with pre-commitments to purchase them if successful.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Concrete policy asks (capital-tax reform, tech antitrust, government AI procurement commitments) that, if adopted, would directly affect capital-vs-labor tax arbitrage and could create a government-backed demand channel for 'pro-worker AI' vendors distinct from AGI-focused labs.

themes.theme: Immigration and AI as flashpoint issues for governability

insights.claim: Acemoglu observes that a majority of western European populations report immigration is too high, yet for many on the left any criticism of immigration is treated as taboo -- exemplifying how cultural-political battlelines have become unbridgeable even on issues with majority public opinion.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Highlights a persistent gap between elite/party discourse and median-voter opinion on immigration across Western Europe, a structural tailwind for populist-right parties in upcoming European elections.

insights.claim: AI regulation has become a marker of identity politics on both sides: for techno-optimists, calls to regulate AI are seen as a moral failure worse than Luddism, while for some progressives resistance to AI itself has become an identity marker -- meaning AI policy debates are increasingly driven by tribal signalling rather than technical assessment.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Suggests AI regulation outcomes in Western democracies will be shaped more by partisan identity dynamics than by evidence-based cost-benefit analysis, adding unpredictability to the regulatory environment relevant for AI company compliance planning.
